title: Question: Layer Norm tutorial 05
body_excerpt: I think I am missing something when going over the Triton implementation of LayerNorm in the tutorial. In the forward, we compute the mean as: ```python _mean = tl.zeros([BLOCK_SIZE], dtype=tl.float32) for off in range(0, N, BLOCK_SIZE): cols = off + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE) a = tl.load(X + cols, mask=cols < N, other=0.).to(tl.float32) _mean += a mean = tl.sum(_mean, axis=0) / N ``` But below, we enforce `N <= BLOCK_SIZE`: ```python if N > BLOCK_SIZE: raise RuntimeError("This layer norm doesn't support feature dim >= 64KB.") ``` So I am a bit confused by the implementation of the forward. Couldn't we do something as simple as: ```python cols = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE) mean = tl.sum(tl.load(X + cols, mask=cols < N, other=0.).to(tl.float32)) / N ``` I think I might be missing a subtlety here. Is there a situation where the more complex implementation in the tutorial is useful, because even if I use a `BLOCK_SIZE < N`, I feel like I would launch more kernels instead of going through the for loop over `range(0, N, BLOCK_SIZE)`. Very curious to have your thoughts, thank you!

body_excerpt: # Feature Request: Expose TTGIR Layout Attributes via Python API ## Summary Add a Python-accessible API to retrieve the `#blocked` (and other) layout attributes assigned during TTGIR compilation, either as a field on `CompiledKernel.metadata` or via a dedicated method on the MLIR module bindings. ## Motivation When performance-debugging Triton kernels, the **layout** assigned to tensors during the TTIR→TTGIR lowering pass is critical information. It determines: - **Vectorization**: `sizePerThread` controls whether the compiler can emit `ld.global.v4.b32` (128-bit vectorized loads) vs scalar loads. This directly affects memory coalescing, bank conflicts in shared memory, and register pressure. - **Number of groups per thread**: When `BLOCK_SIZE > sizePerThread × threadsPerWarp × warpsPerCTA`, each thread processes multiple "groups". title: Refactor precision handling in test/test_optim.py
body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch Currently, there are scattered places in the optimizer tests that reduce precision (grepping for `atol` or `rtol` in the file will take you to those places). Since optimizers are a composition of ATen ops, they reasonably require higher tolerances. Thus, we should establish a per optimizer (and perhaps per dtype) tolerance at the top level of the test file and use that everywhere. This consolidation has (at least) two functions: - Define an agreed upon set of expected tolerances for optimizers - Enable ease when writing new optimizer tests that will inevitably run into the same tolerance issues. One way to do this is to override assertEqual in the Optimizer TestCase class. ### Alternatives Another way is to globally define them and then pass them whenever needed. This seems a more manual way to get the same results as overriding though. ### Additional context I'm in the middle of migrating tests from test/optim/test_optim.py to test/test_optim.py. title: Feature Request: Batched convolve2d
body_excerpt: ### Description Hello, I'd like to request the addition of a batched convolve2d function - one that takes two lists of arrays (or perhaps implemented as two 3D arrays) and convolves them elementwise. Currently, convolve2d can only handle a single pair of 2D arrays. This leaves much parallelism on the table when multiple independent pairs of arrays must be convolved, as each convolution would be executed in serial, rather than parallel. This is particularly impactful for GPU acceleration, as manually issuing multiple convolve2d calls would result in many additional synchronization points, significantly reducing performance compared to if the convolutions were executed in parallel. ### Additional Information _No response_

Polar decomposition is useful in applications like Graphics, Vision, Quantum Computing, among others. It can be used as an alternative to the Newton-Schulz step in the popular Muon optimizer (https://kellerjordan.github.io/posts/muon/). title: [RFC] Remove `cupyx.tools.install_library` in CuPy v14
body_excerpt: CuPy supports several "satellite" CUDA libraries: cuTENSOR, NCCL, and cuDNN. Historically CuPy's binary packages have been built with specific versions of these libraries, and we were asking users to install that version of libraries using `cupyx.tools.install_library` tool, which downloads library archives from NVIDIA website and extract them under `~/.cupy`. However, today these libraries are also available on PyPI (e.g. https://pypi.org/project/cutensor-cu12/ and https://pypi.org/project/nvidia-nccl-cu12/), and it is becoming common to use the PyPI installation among CUDA/Python projects (such as PyTorch). And now that CuPy supports loading both cuTENSOR and NCCL from PyPI wheels (#9201), it does not make much sense to continue providing the tool. Note that cuDNN support is going to be removed as discussed in a separate RFC issue (#8215). Therefore I am thinking of removing the tool in CuPy v14. I believe this doesn't impact most of the use-cases but will keep this RFC issue open for a while to allow anyone to jump in the discussion.

title: RFC: Overlap optimizer computation with DDP/FSDP backward
body_excerpt: with @cbalioglu **Context** Communication/computation overlap is a well-known theme in data parallel training where developers exploit any independence in the forward/backward/optimizer passes of model training and parallelize to increase the performance. Recently there has been some interest in overlapping optimizer computation with DDP backwards to further increase communication/computation overlap. Initial experiments from a prototype that overlaps SGD optimizer step with DDP backwards has shown ~15% peak memory reduction on a few benchmarks, which enables larger model training or larger batch size with the same amount of GPU memory. This is becase peak memory is reduced since the optimizer only needs to load the state of one parameter while doing `step` for that parameter, instead of loading all per-parameter optimizer states into lists prior to running `step()` for all parameters. **Goal** - Enable optimizer overlap with DDP backwards as a prototype feature in Pytorch, after which it can be used to experiment on various workloads with the goal of memory savings and increased efficiency. - Further investigate ZeRO optimizer to see if ZeRO communication can be overlapped with...

title: Feature request: cache autotune timing independent of config list
body_excerpt: When `cache_results` is set for `@triton.autotune` autotune timings are cached to disk to avoid future autotuning, but in the current implementation they are all cached as a single file and the cache key includes the list of configs. This means if you add or remove a config from your autotune list (or alter your `prune_configs_by`) Triton reruns all the autotuning. I propose a more granular caching that does not include the config list and caches the timing for each config separately. Not sure if there's some subtlety I'm missing, but I don't think the other configs present in the autotuner should affect the timing for a given config. Relevant function is: https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/59c9ff171cd3adb5ca057cb40cfbf33bfb4c35ca/python/triton/runtime/autotuner.py#L170-L210

title: Feature request: `DataLoader` using multithreading instead of multiprocessing
body_excerpt: ### Feature request: `DataLoader` using multithreading instead of multiprocessing A version of `DataLoader` that uses **multithreading** would bring several advantages: * Lower inter-process communication and pickling overhead; in some cases this is much faster. See the blogpost by Nvidia showcasing it: https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/improved-data-loading-with-threads/ * Dramatically lower memory usage because threads share address space. * No need to pick between `fork`, `forkserver`, or `spawn` start methods and choosing the disadvantages of one of these. Multiprocessing is mainly used to bypass the GIL, but that argument is weakening: * Many data-loading steps (network I/O, Image decode, decompression) release the GIL anyway, so multiple threads can overlap them. * Starting with Python 3.13 the GIL can be disabled entirely, further reducing the benefit of processes. ### Suggested interface ```python DataLoader( dataset, num_workers=8, worker_backend="thread", # default stays "process" ) ``` cc @andrewkho @divyanshk @SsnL @VitalyFedyunin @dzhulgakov @scotts @albanD @pragupta

title: Fused RNN refactor plan
body_excerpt: This ticket is to track our plan to refactor the fused RNN API (which makes use of the CuDNN implementation of RNNs). **Why is this difficult?** There are a number of factors which make fused RNNs unusual, compared to most of the other differentiable operations in PyTorch * It requires an unusually large, structured series of weights. Most differentiable operators have a fixed number of weights, but an RNN for an entire sequence must have weights for every layer of the RNN. To make matters worse, each layer needs not one but two tensors; the weight and the bias. No other operator in PyTorch behaves like this. * CuDNN requires these weights and inputs to be packed in a particular way. The required packing operations are frequently reported by users as an extremely confusing aspect of PyTorch. * Not only do the weights vary depending on the type of RNN, so do the hidden tensors. If you are an LSTM, you have both hx and cx; for other RNNs, only hx is needed. * RNN with dropout is a stateful API, which requires dropout descriptors to be passed between invocations to handle randomness. **What do we want to do?** Here are the desired goals of the RNN refactor: * Make CuDNN RNN availab...

title: Design API for accessing sparse tensor indices
body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch A sparse tensor can be viewed as a pair of indices and values that define the set of specified tensor elements. PyTorch supports sparse tensors with COO and CSR formats and starting from https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/75831, also CSC, BSR, and BSC formats. All mentioned sparse formats use the `.values()` method to retrieve the values of specified sparse tensor elements. However, the API for accessing the indices of sparse tensor elements lacks uniformity and completeness: - the indices of COO tensors are provided via the `.indices()` method - the indices of CSR and BSR tensors are provided via the `.crow_indices()` and `.col_indices()` methods - the indices of CSC and BSC tensors can be accessed via the `.crow_indices()` and `.col_indices()` methods as a temporary defect. It is a defect because `crow_indices()` returns the compressed column indices and `col_indices()` returns the row indices.
